asr.full_text: I have to say that I really do enjoy playing my Nintendo Switch. That is why one day I thought to myself how awesome would it be to have a device with a similar form factor that cannot only play retro games but can also be used as a Windows 10 tablet. Sadly though such a device does not exist. So I had no other choice than to build one by myself. It can be powered by a USB Type-C PD power source like a power bank, comes with a touch screen to easily control the Windows 10 operating system and also features all important Gamepad buttons which are mandatory for some retro gaming. So sit back and enjoy the journey of me creating this device so that you can easily rebuild it at home. Let's get started... A real job offer, right here in the description. This video is sponsored by JLCPCB which offers cheap but still high quality PCB's, stencils $400 coupons for SMT assembly and PCB prices do as always start at $2 So upload your Gerber files today and try out their service Let's start off with the heart of the system which is this Lattepanda single board computer Now it might not be the cheapest SBC on the market but it certainly comes with rather powerful specifications for its size, has Windows 10 installed, features lots of ports just like a proper computer and even has a built in Arduino which we will later use for the gamepad. To test it all I had to do was to connect 5-volt power source, wait for the red LED to turn off, and then hold the power button until the red LED starts glowing again. But obviously I forgot all about a display for this mini computer. For that I got myself this Waveshare 7-inch HDMI LCD with integrated capacitive touch screen It's price was once again, not that low but I have to say that it's picture quality is pretty good The touch screen works perfectly and it even comes with an audio power amplifier which we will later use to add a small speaker to the gaming system So next I use this small and flat HDMI cable to connect the display to the Latte Panda. Used a Micro USB cable to connect the touch port of the Display to a USB port of the Latte Panda and finally used another Micro USB cable hooked up to the power only port which I connected to a separate 5V Power Source. But since I later only want to use one 5V power source for the gaming system which powers both the Latte Panda and the screen I cut up both power wires, removed the insulation of the red 5V and Black Ground wire, grabbed myself a microUSB breakout board and soldered O4 wires to the corresponding 5V or Ground Pads. After then plugging this microUSB breakout in only one power source, we can see that the system does work just fine… at least until a certain point since the combined current draw of both devices exceed the current capabilities of our power source and since I later want to power the system with a power bank which comes with the same current limit of two amps we might have a serious problem here. Thankfully though, I got one of those USB type C PD PCBs laying around which I presented you in one of my previous videos about USB type C. Simply put, by using a USB type C cable and a compatible USB type C PD power bank we can get 3A of current instead of just 2. So I soldered all wires of the system to this circuit, powered it up and as you can see this time everything works without problems. And after confirming that all functions of Windows 10 work flawlessly by also watching some of my own videos I went over to the RetroArch website which is the software that I will be using for the retrogaming aspect. Now I will not go into detail here on how to setup this software because honestly speaking, there are already enough videos about that topic. But as soon as you are basically done with setting the software up you can use a keyboard to play some retro games like for example Goden Axe right here. Needless to say though we cannot fit a keyboard into our target form factor which is why we can also hook up a simple gamepad, map its entire buttons and use that as an input controller. But I really didn't feel like dealing with the Gamepad PCB and buttons which is why I had a closer look at the Arduino of the Lattepanda and realised that it uses the Atmega32u4 Which is also used in the Arduino Leonardo Which coincidentally can also act as a gamepad So I installed the Arduino joystick library And used it to write a bit of code which maps the different pins of the Atmega I see to a button of the gamepad After then opening the sketch on the LatePanda, selecting the Arduino Leonardo as a target, and uploading it, it seems like a new gamepad got successfully recognised! Here you can see which pin of the LatePanda Arduino acts as which button. And after soldering wires to a tactile push button and hooking it up between one of the shown pins and grounds you can see that Windows successfully detects the button push and thus we can use it in the RetroArch software. The last two components we need for the hardware setup are a small speaker and a 3.5mm audio jack. The audio jack will later be mounted inside the housing of the game console and wired up to the Late panda audio jack which means it can be used to plug in headphones. The speaker will obviously also later be secured inside the housing and Directly hooked up to the screens audio amplifier through the help of its included connector wire It's volume can then easily get adjusted through the push buttons mounted on the screens PCB but wait a minute That means those push buttons along with the LATEPANDA's power button also needs a tactile push button extension mounted inside the housing And that was the point I started creating a couple of sketches How the game console should look like? and where all the mandatory components should be placed With those blueprints in mind I started creating 3D models of all the important components with their mounting holes in Fusion 360. To do that, I either had to manually measure the components or use the dimensions I found on the internet. And with those models, I was not only able to figure out the size of the game console But I was also able to create precise mounting holes for all of them And after 50 versions of my design and around 10 hours This was the housing I was finally happy with So I printed its upper half with black PLA filaments Its lower half with white filaments And all the button caps, shoulder pads and holding parts With red filaments As soon as I got all the 3D printed parts I removed their support material Did a bit of extra treatment for some sections And started the assembly by grabbing dozens of 9.5mm long tactile push buttons and soldering two wires to each of them. After that was done I positioned the 3D printed button caps inside their holes, pushed the tactile switches into them for which I also later used a bit of hot glue, created a common ground for all the buttons and used a mounting plate and M3 screws in order to tighten it all to the housing. You need to fine adjust the distance of the mounting plate until you get a satisfying button push. I then repeated this process for the other side as well as for all the buttons of the screen and the Latte Panda power button. Next I hot glued a tactile push button near each shoulder pad, and double checked whether they would mechanically work later on, which they did. At this point I secured the speaker, USB Type-C PD PCB and audio jack inside the housing with a bit of two component adhesive. Then I finally secured the latte panda as well as the screen in place with more M3 screws, added male headers to the latte panda arduino and wired up most of the buttons to it. The rest got connected to the screen or the Latte Panda power button. But do not worry if you didn't get all the details because you can find more pictures and information about this project as always in the video description. After wiring up the audio jack and speaker, it was time to solder the Latte Panda Micro USB cable to power from which I used another chopped up USB cable to power the screen. As you can see there was a lack of space which also forced me to directly solder the data wires of the touch ports to another USB cable which then got plugged into the LATTE PANDA and just like that the electrical wiring was complete which means it was time to close the system up and use more M3 screws to hold the two halves together. And as you can see by powering it with the power bank, it all still works just fine. I hope you enjoyed this project and maybe I even inspired you to create something similar. If so don't forget to like, share, subscribe and hit the notification bell Stay creative and I will see you next time!

So sit back and enjoy the journey of me creating this device so that you can easily rebuild it at home. Let's get started... A real job offer, right here in the description. This video is sponsored by JLCPCB which offers cheap but still high quality PCB's, stencils $400 coupons for SMT assembly and PCB prices do as always start at $2 So upload your Gerber files today and try out their service Let's start off with the heart of the system which is this Lattepanda single board computer Now it might not be the cheapest SBC on the market but it certainly comes with rather powerful specifications for its size, has Windows 10 installed, features lots of ports just like a proper computer and even has a built in Arduino which we will later use for the gamepad. To test it all I had to do was to connect 5-volt power source, wait for the red LED to turn off, and then hold the power button until the red LED starts glowing again. But obviously I forgot all about a display for this mini computer. For that I got

myself this Waveshare 7-inch HDMI LCD with integrated capacitive touch screen It's price was once again, not that low but I have to say that it's picture quality is pretty good The touch screen works perfectly and it even comes with an audio power amplifier which we will later use to add a small speaker to the gaming system So next I use this small and flat HDMI cable to connect the display to the Latte Panda. Used a Micro USB cable to connect the touch port of the Display to a USB port of the Latte Panda and finally used another Micro USB cable hooked up to the power only port which I connected to a separate 5V Power Source. But since I later only want to use one 5V power source for the gaming system which powers both the Latte Panda and the screen I cut up both power wires, removed the insulation of the red 5V and Black Ground wire, grabbed myself a microUSB breakout board and soldered O4 wires to the corresponding 5V or Ground Pads. After then plugging this microUSB breakout in only one power source, we can see that the system does work just fine… at least until a certain point since the combined current draw of both devices exceed the current capabilities of our power source and since I later want to power the system with a power bank which comes with the same current limit of two amps we might have a serious problem here. Thankfully though, I got one of those USB type C PD PCBs laying around which I presented you in one of my previous videos about USB type C. Simply put, by using a USB type C cable and a compatible USB type C PD power bank we can get 3A of current

instead of just 2. So I soldered all wires of the system to this circuit, powered it up and as you can see this time everything works without problems. And after confirming that all functions of Windows 10 work flawlessly by also watching some of my own videos I went over to the RetroArch website which is the software that I will be using for the retrogaming aspect. Now I will not go into detail here on how to setup this software because honestly speaking, there are already enough videos about that topic. But as soon as you are basically done with setting the software up you can use a keyboard to play some retro games like for example Goden Axe right here. Needless to say though we cannot fit a keyboard into our target form factor which is why we can also hook up a simple gamepad, map its entire buttons and use that as an input controller. But I really didn't feel like dealing with the Gamepad PCB and buttons which is why I had a closer look at the Arduino of the Lattepanda and realised that it uses the Atmega32u4 Which is also used in the Arduino Leonardo Which coincidentally can also act as a gamepad So I installed the Arduino joystick library And used it to write a bit of code which maps the different pins of the Atmega I see to a button of the gamepad After then opening the sketch on the LatePanda, selecting the Arduino Leonardo as a target, and uploading it, it seems like a new gamepad got successfully recognised! Here you can see which pin of the LatePanda Arduino acts as which button. And after soldering wires to a tactile push button and hooking it up between one

of the shown pins and grounds you can see that Windows successfully detects the button push and thus we can use it in the RetroArch software. The last two components we need for the hardware setup are a small speaker and a 3.5mm audio jack. The audio jack will later be mounted inside the housing of the game console and wired up to the Late panda audio jack which means it can be used to plug in headphones. The speaker will obviously also later be secured inside the housing and Directly hooked up to the screens audio amplifier through the help of its included connector wire It's volume can then easily get adjusted through the push buttons mounted on the screens PCB but wait a minute That means those push buttons along with the LATEPANDA's power button also needs a tactile push button extension mounted inside the housing And that was the point I started creating a couple of sketches How the game console should look like? and where all the mandatory components should be placed With those blueprints in mind I started creating 3D models of all the important components with their mounting holes in Fusion 360. To do that, I either had to manually measure the components or use the dimensions I found on the internet. And with those models, I was not only able to figure out the size of the game console But I was also able to create precise mounting holes for all of them And after 50 versions of my design and around 10 hours This was the housing I was finally happy with So I printed its upper half with black PLA filaments Its lower half with white filaments And all the button caps,

shoulder pads and holding parts With red filaments As soon as I got all the 3D printed parts I removed their support material Did a bit of extra treatment for some sections And started the assembly by grabbing dozens of 9.5mm long tactile push buttons and soldering two wires to each of them. After that was done I positioned the 3D printed button caps inside their holes, pushed the tactile switches into them for which I also later used a bit of hot glue, created a common ground for all the buttons and used a mounting plate and M3 screws in order to tighten it all to the housing. You need to fine adjust the distance of the mounting plate until you get a satisfying button push. I then repeated this process for the other side as well as for all the buttons of the screen and the Latte Panda power button. Next I hot glued a tactile push button near each shoulder pad, and double checked whether they would mechanically work later on, which they did. At this point I secured the speaker, USB Type-C PD PCB and audio jack inside the housing with a bit of two component adhesive. Then I finally secured the latte panda as well as the screen in place with more M3 screws, added male headers to the latte panda arduino and wired up most of the buttons to it. The rest got connected to the screen or the Latte Panda power button. But do not worry if you didn't get all the details because you can find more pictures and information about this project as always in the video description. After wiring up the audio jack and speaker, it was time to solder the Latte Panda Micro USB cable to power from

which I used another chopped up USB cable to power the screen. As you can see there was a lack of space which also forced me to directly solder the data wires of the touch ports to another USB cable which then got plugged into the LATTE PANDA and just like that the electrical wiring was complete which means it was time to close the system up and use more M3 screws to hold the two halves together. And as you can see by powering it with the power bank, it all still works just fine. I hope you enjoyed this project and maybe I even inspired you to create something similar. If so don't forget to like, share, subscribe and hit the notification bell Stay creative and I will see you next time!
